extracted.intended_audience: students, economists, and policymakers interested in political economy and trade policy
extracted.subtask_description: Critical evaluation of export/production bounties, corn trade regulations, and related mercantilist policies — their economic effects, distributional consequences, and perverse incentives. The rubric collects the criteria Adam Smith uses to judge such policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forcing industry into less advantageous channels
rubrics_metrics.description: All the different expedients of the mercantile system force some part of the industry of the country into a channel less advantageous than that in which it would run of its own accord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a bounty or regulation diverts labor and capital away from their naturally most productive uses — a general objection applicable to bounties upon exportation and similar mercantile measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the policy increase real production (not just nominal price)?
rubrics_metrics.description: The bounty upon the exportation of corn can in no respect promote the raising of that particular commodity of which it was meant to encourage the production; it raises the nominal, not the real price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the measure enables the producer to maintain and employ more labour (real value), not merely to receive a higher money price. If it only raises nominal prices, it does not increase real production or employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish real value from nominal money price
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the real, but the nominal price of corn, which can in any considerable degree be affected by the bounty. The real effect of the bounty is to degrade the real value of silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess policies by their effect on purchasing power and real wages, not just monetary prices. Policies that raise nominal prices but lower purchasing power are largely illusory in benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-run effects on population, industry, and home market
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary exportation of corn occasioned by the bounty ... must so far tend to restrain the industry of the country; its final tendency is to stint and restrain the gradual extension of the home market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider cumulative, long-term impacts: whether a policy reduces domestic industry, restrains population growth (via reduced sustenance), or diminishes the domestic market's expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on relative prices and international competitiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The bounty renders our corn somewhat dearer in the home market and somewhat cheaper in the foreign; it tends to render our manufactures somewhat dearer in every market, and theirs somewhat cheaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a subsidy makes domestic manufactures less competitive abroad (and at home) by altering relative prices, enabling foreign competitors to undersell domestic producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beneficiary identification and distributional consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: There is perhaps but one set of men ... to whom the bounty either was or could be essentially serviceable. These were the corn merchants, the exporters and importers of corn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify who actually benefits (merchants, exporters, producers, landlords). Policies that largely reward intermediaries rather than producers or public welfare are suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perverse incentives from payment basis (tonnage vs output)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tonnage bounty ... is proportioned to the burden of the ship, not to her diligence or success in the fishery; it has ... been too common for the vessels to fit out for the sole purpose of catching, not the fish but the bounty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design subsidies to be tied to productive output or success, not fixed characteristics that can be gamed. Watch for payments that encourage rent-seeking or meaningless scaling of capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of encouraged methods to local conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The mode of fishing for which this tonnage bounty ... has been given (busses or decked vessels ...) seems not so well adapted to the situation of Scotland ... A boat-fishery seems to be the mode of fishing best adapted to the peculiar situation of Scotland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the policy encourages techniques or business forms appropriate to local geography, resources, and traditional comparative advantages, or whether it imports inappropriate methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether a trade becomes dependent on the bounty (losing trade)
rubrics_metrics.description: The trade which cannot be carried on but by means of a bounty being necessarily a losing trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a business is only viable with continued subsidy, it may be inherently unprofitable and a poor public investment. Evaluate profitability absent the bounty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative costs, smuggling, and enforcement consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Spain by taxing, and Portugal by prohibiting, the exportation of gold and silver, load that exportation with the expense of smuggling ... The prohibition of exportation cannot detain a greater quantity ... than what the annual produce ... will allow them to employ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for enforcement costs, smuggling incentives, and economic waste caused by prohibitions or heavy taxation that distort flows and create black markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal smoothing: does policy prevent plenty from relieving scarcity later?
rubrics_metrics.description: By hindering the plenty of the one year from relieving the scarcity of another, it occasioned in years of scarcity a greater importation than would otherwise have been necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether measures distort the ability of inventories and trade to smooth interannual fluctuations; subsidies that encourage export of surpluses may worsen future scarcities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between drawbacks and true bounties
rubrics_metrics.description: What is called a bounty, is sometimes no more than a drawback ... those allowances only are called drawbacks which are given upon goods exported in the same form in which they are imported. When that form ... is called a bounty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify supports correctly: drawbacks (refunds of duties on re-exported goods) have different objections than open bounties; evaluate according to nature, not the name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer targeted premiums for excellence over broad bounties
rubrics_metrics.description: Premiums given by the public to artists and manufacturers, who excel in their particular occupations, are not liable to the same objections as bounties. By encouraging extraordinary dexterity and ingenuity, they serve to keep up the emulation of the workmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When supporting industry, consider small, targeted awards that raise skill and quality (low distortion, low cost) rather than large bounties that distort industry allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effectiveness and scale of bounties
rubrics_metrics.description: The bounty upon corn alone has sometimes cost the public, in one year, more than £300,000. The herring-buss bounty seems too large ... each barrel ... cost government ... £113:15s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the fiscal cost per unit of output and compare to market prices; large absolute or per-unit fiscal costs indicate poor value for public spending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic/defense justification as an exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If any particular manufacture was necessary, indeed, for the defence of the society, it might not always be prudent to depend upon our neighbours for the supply ... The bounties upon the exportation of British made sail-cloth, and British made gunpowder, may, perhaps, both be vindicated upon this principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow narrow exceptions where national defense or critical strategic needs justify support that would otherwise be objectionable; require strong evidence of necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Susceptibility to fraud and abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Bounties upon exportation have been abused, to many fraudulent purposes ... Bounties upon production ... have been found by experience more liable to frauds than those upon exportation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine administrative vulnerability to fraud and the practical record of abuses; prefer mechanisms with lower opportunities for cheating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on the distribution of domestic consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: In many parts of Scotland, during certain seasons of the year, herrings make no inconsiderable part of the food of the common people. A bounty which tended to lower their price ... might contribute a good deal to the relief of a great number of our fellow-subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a measure helps or harms domestic consumers, especially poorer populations who depend on certain staples; check whether the support instead channels output abroad or raises home prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design subsidy type according to objective (production vs exportation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To encourage the production of any commodity, a bounty upon production, one should imagine, would have a more direct operation than one upon exportation. It would, besides, impose only one tax upon the people ... Instead of raising, it would tend to lower the price of the commodity in the home market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the instrument to the goal: use production subsidies to increase domestic supply and lower home prices; export subsidies mainly shift sales abroad and can have perverse domestic effects.
